report:
## Conclusion: No — hydroxychloroquine does not reduce the likelihood of dying from COVID-19

The evidence from multiple large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and meta-analyses consistently shows that hydroxychloroquine provides no mortality benefit for COVID-19 patients, and some analyses suggest it may even increase mortality risk.

### Key Evidence

1. **RECOVERY Trial (NEJM, 2020):** The largest RCT, conducted in the UK, randomly assigned 1,561 hospitalized COVID-19 patients to hydroxychloroquine and 3,132 to usual care. It found **no significant difference in 28-day mortality** between the groups, leading the trial to be halted. ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926](https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926))

2. **WHO Solidarity Trial:** The World Health Organization discontinued its hydroxychloroquine arm after data "showed that hydroxychloroquine does not result in the reduction of mortality of hospitalised COVID-19 patients." ([https://www.yahoo.com/news/halts-trial-hydroxychloroquine-covid-19-163503484.html](https://www.yahoo.com/news/halts-trial-hydroxychloroquine-covid-19-163503484.html))

3. **International Collaborative Meta-Analysis (Nature Communications, 2021):** A meta-analysis of published and unpublished RCTs found that hydroxychloroquine treatment for COVID-19 was actually **associated with increased mortality**, and the drug showed no clinical benefit. ([https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z))

4. **JAMA RCT (2020):** A randomized trial comparing hydroxychloroquine vs. placebo in hospitalized adults found **no significant difference in clinical status at 14 days**, including no mortality benefit. ([https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2772922](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2772922))

### Summary

Across large, well-designed RCTs and systematic reviews, hydroxychloroquine consistently failed to reduce death from COVID-19. Some evidence even pointed to harm, likely due to cardiac side effects. Your assessment that the answer is "no" is well supported by the totality of high-quality evidence.
